passage:
“We lost by two points,” Baljeet said, dropping his bag. “It's my fault. I missed the last shot.”

“Baljeet,” said Sangeeta, the captain, “I called the last play. I chose to give you the ball because the defenders were on Ritu. That's on me too.”

“But I missed.”

“And Ritu ran eight minutes of defence, Farah scored twelve, and you made five assists. That's how we got to the last shot at all.”

Farah smiled. Ritu looked up. “I was tired in the last quarter. I should have said I needed a rest.”

“Then we all learn,” said Sangeeta. “Next practice: last-play drills, and anyone can call for a sub.”

Baljeet let out a breath. “Okay.”

qa.q: By how many points did the team lose?
qa.a: The team lost by two points.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta say the last play was “on me too”?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt protective of Baljeet and responsible as captain, since Sangeeta called the play and chose to give Baljeet the ball.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta decide for the next practice?
qa.a: Sangeeta decided on last-play drills and said anyone can call for a sub.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt after Sangeeta listed what each player did?
qa.a: Baljeet probably felt relieved and less alone with the blame, seeing that the effort counted too.

grounding: A team captain acknowledges each member's role and takes a share of the blame in a loss, so mistakes feel safe to admit.

passage:
I'm Nirmala, and I captained our school basketball team last year. We won the district game by one point, and afterwards everyone congratulated me. I felt strange, because I hadn't scored much. In the huddle I said, “Sahil's blocks kept us in it. Farida hit the last shot. Meera's passes did the rest.” Sahil looked down and grinned.

Two weeks later we lost badly. Someone whispered that Sahil had missed too many rebounds. I stood up and said, “I called the wrong plays in the second half. That's mine.” The room went quiet, then Sahil said, “I lost a few rebounds too.” It was the first time anyone on our team admitted a mistake out loud. After that it felt safe to say it.

qa.q: By how many points did the team win the district game?
qa.a: The team won the district game by one point.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala feel strange after the win, when everyone congratulated Nirmala?
qa.a: Nirmala felt uneasy taking the praise alone, having not scored much and seeing the credit as belonging to the team's blocks, shot and passes.

qa.q: What choice did Nirmala make after the heavy loss?
qa.a: Nirmala stood up and said the wrong plays in the second half were Nirmala's own, instead of letting the blame fall on Sahil.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt when the whisper about rebounds turned into Nirmala taking the blame?
qa.a: Sahil probably felt relieved and safe enough to admit lost rebounds too.

grounding: A team captain names each member's role in a win and takes a share of blame in a loss, making mistakes safe to admit.

passage:
Basketball coach's note, U-17 girls, after the district semi-final.
We won by four points. In the huddle, Jaya, our captain, named every player. “Priya, your defence in the last minute. Neha, your two free throws. Even the bench, your shouting helped.” Several girls went red and grinned.
Last month, when we lost the league match, Jaya did the opposite of blaming. She said, “I called the wrong play twice. That's on me.” After that, Kiran, our shooting guard, admitted she'd missed the plan in the second half. Nobody had to be told off.
Madhav, my assistant coach, has noticed players now admit mistakes quickly at practice. I'll ask Jaya to lead the team review each week.

qa.q: By how many points did the team win?
qa.a: By four points.

qa.q: How did the players seem to feel when Jaya named each of them?
qa.a: They seemed pleased and a bit embarrassed, going red and grinning at being recognised.

qa.q: Why does Jaya's way of sharing credit and blame help the team?
qa.a: Praising everyone after a win and owning her mistake after a loss makes it safe for others to admit errors too.

qa.q: How might Kiran have felt admitting she missed the plan?
qa.a: She probably felt nervous but safe to speak, since the captain had admitted her own mistake first.

grounding: A coach notes a captain who credits every member after a win and takes a share of blame in a loss, making mistakes safe to admit.

passage:
Saturday
We lost the inter-school quiz final today by five points. I'm the captain, so I felt it the most.
On the bus back, everyone was quiet. Tanvir had passed on the space question, and he knew it. Everyone knew it. Some of the boys were looking at him.
I stood up. “Okay. I buzzed too early on the history round. That's five points right there. It's on me as much as anyone.”
Tanvir looked up. After a while, he said, “I should have taken the space question. I knew it.”
Then Rhea said she'd second-guessed the geography answer. Suddenly everyone was laughing about our mistakes.
Last month, when we won, I made sure to thank each person by name. I think that helped today.
Ganga

qa.q: By how many points did the team lose?
qa.a: By five points.

qa.q: How did Tanvir seem to feel on the bus before Ganga spoke?
qa.a: He seemed ashamed and anxious, knowing he'd passed on the space question while others looked at him.

qa.q: Why did Ganga admitting a mistake first work?
qa.a: It showed that mistakes were safe to admit, so Tanvir and others owned theirs instead of carrying blame alone.

qa.q: How might Rhea have felt after sharing her mistake?
qa.a: She probably felt relieved and lighter, laughing along with the team.

grounding: A captain writes about taking a share of the blame after a loss, after crediting each member in a win, making mistakes safe to admit.

passage:
The volleyball court behind the Champhai school was still muddy from rain when the girls lost the district semi-final, 21–25 in the last set. Nobody spoke on the walk to the bus. Lalremsiami, who had missed the last serve, kept her face to the window.
Vinita, the captain, stood at the front of the rattling bus. "That last set is on me. I called the wrong rotation and put Mawii out of position. We'll fix it in practice." Then she went down the aisle. "Mawii, your blocks in the first set were unreal. Lalremsiami, your serves won us the quarter-final. Tlangi, you kept us calm."
Lalremsiami looked up. "I missed the last one."
"And I put you in a bad spot to serve it," Vinita said. "We lost together."
At practice on Monday, Mawii was the first to say, "I think I'm late on my jumps. Can we work on that?"

qa.q: What was the score in the last set?
qa.a: 21–25 in the last set.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami keeping her face to the window suggest?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt ashamed and guilty about missing the last serve, expecting to be blamed.

qa.q: What did Vinita get right as captain?
qa.a: She took her share of the blame first, praised each player's specific part, and told Lalremsiami they lost together.

qa.q: What does Mawii's question on Monday show about how the team feels now?
qa.a: Mawii feels safe to admit a weakness, because the captain showed that mistakes can be named without shame 🙂

grounding: Shows a team captain crediting each member and taking a share of the blame after a loss, which makes mistakes safe to admit.
